title: Housing
summary: Hutch design, ventilation, space and bedding.
points: Give each rabbit enough space to stretch fully, stand on its hind legs and move around comfortably.
Raise hutches off the ground to keep rabbits dry and to make cleaning underneath easier.
Make sure hutches are well ventilated but shielded from direct wind, rain and strong sun.
Use dry bedding (straw or wood shavings) and change it regularly to keep the hutch clean.
Provide a separate nest box for does that are due to kindle, lined with soft bedding.
Keep hutches away from loud noise and predators, and check wire mesh regularly for damage.

title: Feeding
summary: Feed types, fodder, water and feeding routines.
points: Offer a mix of good-quality hay or dry fodder, fresh greens, and a balanced commercial pellet where available.
Introduce new feeds gradually — sudden changes can upset a rabbit's digestion.
Always provide clean, fresh drinking water, checked at least once a day.
Feed at consistent times each day so rabbits settle into a routine.
Avoid mouldy, wilted or pesticide-treated greens, and avoid overfeeding rich foods.
Kits (young rabbits) need access to their mother's milk and, from a few weeks old, small amounts of solid feed alongside it.

title: Breeding
summary: Selecting stock, mating, pregnancy, kindling and kits.
points: Choose healthy, mature does and bucks in good body condition for breeding.
Introduce the doe to the buck's hutch (not the other way round) and supervise the initial mating.
Pregnancy (gestation) typically lasts around a month — prepare a clean nest box a few days before it is due.
Reduce handling and disturbance in the days just before and after kindling (giving birth).
Check the nest for kits daily but keep handling brief and calm, especially in the first days.
Kits are usually weaned gradually from about 4-6 weeks, once they are eating solid food well.

title: Hygiene & Health
summary: Cleaning, isolation, observation and when to seek help.
points: Clean hutches and feeding equipment regularly to prevent the build-up of droppings and damp bedding.
Observe each rabbit daily for changes in appetite, droppings, coat condition or behaviour.
Isolate any rabbit that appears unwell from the rest of the group to reduce the risk of spreading illness.
Keep new arrivals separate for a short period before introducing them to your existing rabbits.
Seek advice from a qualified veterinary officer promptly if a rabbit seems seriously unwell — this guide is general information, not a diagnosis.
Keep the area around hutches free of standing water and rotting waste to discourage pests.

title: Farm Management
summary: Identification, records, and tracking your stock.
points: Give each rabbit a simple ID (for example ARF-001) so you can track it in your records.
Keep a basic breeding record: which doe and buck were paired, and the expected kindling date.
Record feeding costs, sales and other expenses so you know whether the farm is profitable.
Track mortality and its likely causes so you can spot recurring problems early.
Review your records periodically to decide which rabbits to keep for breeding and which to sell.

title: Marketing
summary: Finding buyers, pricing and selling farm by-products.
points: Be clear and honest in your listings about a rabbit's age, sex, colour and health.
Prices vary by age, sex and purpose (young stock vs. proven breeding stock) — review similar local listings before setting yours.
Manure and urine can be sold separately to farmers and gardeners as a steady side income.
Word of mouth and clear WhatsApp communication go a long way for a small farm — respond to enquiries promptly.
Keep photos honest and up to date, and update a listing's status as soon as a rabbit is reserved or sold.
